extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Kantian aesthetics; scholars of philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted criteria for forming and evaluating aesthetic judgements (taste, beauty, the sublime, teleological vs aesthetic judgements) as presented in Kant's Critique of Judgment with editorial notes and examples. Useful for applying Kantian standards to artworks, nature, and aesthetic discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste (faculty of judging the beautiful)
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition of taste which is laid down here is that it is the faculty of judging of the beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analysis of judgements of taste must show what is required in order to call an object beautiful. The moments to which this judgement has regard in its reflection are sought according to the guidance of the logical functions of judgement; in a judgement of taste a reference to the Understanding is always involved. The aesthetical judgement first pays attention to the moment of quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinterestedness of aesthetic judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: A judgement upon an object of satisfaction may be quite disinterested; judgements of taste do not in themselves establish any interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A pure aesthetic judgement must be 'disinterested' — not based upon an interest in the object. Such disinterestedness is broader than merely lacking a desire to possess the object; it excludes that the judgement be determined by concepts of the object or by sensations that serve as determining grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for claiming universal assent for an aesthetical judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: To be justified in claiming universal assent for an aesthetical judgement that rests merely on subjective grounds, it is sufficient to assume (1) that the subjective conditions of the Judgement ... are the same in all men, and (2) the judgement must merely have reference to this relation (consequently to the formal condition of the Judgement) and be pure, i.e. not mingled either with concepts of the Object or with sensations, as determining grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the judgement is mixed with concepts or sensations, the privileged claim to universal assent is misapplied. The two conditions explain how a merely subjective aesthetic judgement can still lawfully claim universal communicability ('sensus communis aestheticus').

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposiveness without purpose (formal purposiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: A thing can be regarded as beautiful because in perceiving it we find a certain purposiveness which, in our judgement, is referred to no purpose at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beauty arises from perceived purposiveness of form when we do not refer that form to any definite purpose (example: a tulip regarded as beautiful because its form shows purposiveness without reference to a purpose). This contrasts with artefacts whose apparent purposiveness is taken as referring to an intended function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between aesthetical and teleological judgements
rubrics_metrics.description: In the aesthetical part we view beautiful nature with favour and have a free (disinterested) satisfaction in its form. But in a teleological judgement we pay attention to this reference [to purpose], and here we can regard it as a favour of nature that it has been willing to minister to our culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic judgements are concerned with form and disinterested pleasure; teleological judgements attend to purposes and the role of natural purposiveness in relation to ends (e.g., nature as 'favouring' human culture). They are different kinds of reflective judgement and should not be conflated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Models of taste should be composed in dead and learned languages
rubrics_metrics.description: Models of taste as regards the arts of speech must be composed in a dead and learned language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons: (1) dead languages do not suffer the change that living languages undergo (noble expressions becoming flat, etc.), and (2) learned languages have a grammar subject to no wanton change of fashion, preserving rules unchanged. This is a practical guideline for constructing lasting exemplars of literary taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regularity, characteristic, and caricature in artistic representation
rubrics_metrics.description: A perfectly regular countenance ordinarily tells us nothing because it contains nothing characteristic and therefore rather expresses the Idea of the race than the specific traits of a person; the exaggeration of a characteristic which does violence to the normal Idea is called caricature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A regular/model countenance may indicate a mediocre person; genius often departs from ordinary relations of faculties in favour of some special one. Caricature exaggerates characteristics beyond the normal idea; artists seeking to express individuality should avoid mere regularity or grotesque violation of the ideal form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affections vs passions with respect to the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: Affections are specifically different from passions: the former are related merely to feeling; the latter belong to the faculty of desire and are inclinations which render difficult or impossible the determination of the will by principles. The latter can never and in no reference be called sublime; because while in an affection the freedom of the mind is hindered, in a passion it is abolished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For the experience of the sublime, emotions that hinder free reflection (affections) may contribute, but passions — steady, determining inclinations that abolish freedom — cannot ground the sublime. This distinguishes affective states admissible in sublime judgement from disqualifying passions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic judgement involves reference to the Understanding (reflective relation)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a judgement of taste a reference to the Understanding is always involved; the moments to which this judgement has regard in its reflection are sought in accordance with the guidance of the logical functions of judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant uses logical-functional analysis to isolate the 'moments' in aesthetic reflection (quality is primary). This methodological criterion: analyse aesthetic judgements by considering how cognitive faculties (imagination, understanding) are put into play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of the fine arts by relation to concept and imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Landscape gardening may be regarded as a species of the art of painting ... since it actually takes its forms from nature and has no concept of the object and its purpose (as in Architecture), but involves merely the free play of the Imagination in contemplation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for classifying arts: whether the art takes forms from nature or from conceptual/purpose-driven design, and whether it involves free play of imagination (aesthetic painting, landscape gardening) or definite purpose (architecture). Use this to group arts under the principle of expression of aesthetical Ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beautiful speech vs manipulative rhetoric (criterion for oratory as art)
rubrics_metrics.description: Readiness and accuracy in speaking (which together constitute Rhetoric) belong to beautiful art; but the art of the orator (ars oratoria), the art of availing oneself of the weaknesses of men for one's own designs ... is worthy of no respect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between the aesthetic excellence of speech (style, imaginative presentation) and rhetorical manipulation aimed at moving people for ulterior ends. The former can be 'beautiful art'; the latter is morally suspect and not to be admired as true aesthetic achievement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for attributing purposiveness in artefacts vs natural objects
rubrics_metrics.description: If we regard a thing as a work of art, that is enough to make us admit that its shape has reference to some design and definite purpose. Hence there is no immediate satisfaction in the contemplation of it. On the other hand a flower is regarded as beautiful because in perceiving it we find a certain purposiveness which, in our judgement, is referred to no purpose at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use whether we conceive an object as designed (artifact) or not (natural object) to determine whether purposiveness produces immediate aesthetic satisfaction (formal purposiveness) or calls for teleological interpretation tied to function.
